rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: The parallelogram law gives a different result from the triangle law — They give identical results. The triangle is simply half the parallelogram. The diagonal of the parallelogram is the third side of the triangle.  ·  The angle in the formula is the interior angle of the parallelogram — The angle $\theta$ in $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$ is the angle between the two vectors when placed tail-to-tail, which equals the interior angle at the common vertex.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Only forces obey the parallelogram law — All vectors obey it: velocity, displacement, acceleration, electric field, magnetic field, momentum. Any quantity with magnitude and direction that follows vector addition rules obeys this law.  ·  The resultant is always the longer diagonal — No. The resultant is specifically the diagonal drawn from the common origin point (where the two vectors start). The other diagonal represents $\vec{P}-\vec{Q}$.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Newton's **second law of motion** ($\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$) implicitly relies on the parallelogram law: the net force is the vector sum of all individual forces, found by successive application of the parallelogram law.  ·  The **parallelogram identity** ($|\vec{A}+\vec{B}|^2 + |\vec{A}-\vec{B}|^2 = 2|\vec{A}|^2 + 2|\vec{B}|^2$) is a fundamental property of inner product spaces and holds in any number of dimensions, not just 2D.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Statement**: If two vectors acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram drawn from that point, their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram passing through the same point.  ·  **Setup**: let $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ be two vectors acting at point $A$, represented by adjacent sides $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AD}$ of parallelogram $ABCD$. The diagonal $\vec{AC}$ represents the resultant $\vec{R}$. The angle between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ is $\theta$.  ·  **Derivation of magnitude**: draw $CE$ perpendicular to $AB$ extended. In right triangle $BCE$: $CE = Q\sin\theta$ and $BE = Q\cos\theta$. Then $AE = AB + BE = P + Q\cos\theta$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws of vectors and other topics  ·  Key Formula 5: Important relation in Triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws of vectors  ·  If $\theta = 90°$, the parallelogram becomes a square — It becomes a **rectangle**, not necessarily a square. It is a square only if $P = Q$ as well.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The direction formula changes between the two laws — The direction formula $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(Q\sin\theta/(P+Q\cos\theta))$ is identical for both the triangle and parallelogram laws, since they are geometrically equivalent.  ·  You need to draw a full parallelogram to use the law — No. You can use just the triangle (half the parallelogram) for calculations. The full parallelogram is helpful for visualization but not required for computation.  ·  The parallelogram law and triangle law are different — They are mathematically identical. The triangle is exactly half the parallelogram. Both give the same $R$ and $\alpha$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The parallelogram law fails for three or more vectors — It extends naturally: for three vectors, first find $\vec{R}_{12} = \vec{P}+\vec{Q}$ using the parallelogram, then combine $\vec{R}_{12}$ with $\vec{R}$ using the law again. Or use the polygon law for 3+ vectors directly.  ·  The angle $\theta$ in the formula is the angle inside the triangle — $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors when placed tail-to-tail, NOT the interior angle of the triangle. If the interior angle is $\phi$, then $\theta = 180° - \phi$.  ·  The resultant always points between the two vectors — This is only true for $0° < \theta < 180°$. When vectors are opposite ($\theta=180°$), the resultant lies along the larger vector, not between them.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Triangle law only works for forces — Triangle law applies to ALL vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, electric field, magnetic field, momentum. Any quantity that is a vector obeys this law.  ·  If the triangle doesn't close, the vectors are wrong — An open triangle means the resultant is the closing side. The triangle law says the resultant IS the third side taken in the opposite order — the triangle is open by design.  ·  The direction formula $\tan\alpha = Q\sin\theta/(P+Q\cos\theta)$ is only for the triangle law — This formula is actually derived from the triangle law but is identical to the one from the parallelogram law. Both methods give the same $\alpha$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A zero resultant means the triangle has no area — A zero resultant means the two vectors are equal and opposite ($P=Q$, $\theta=180°$), forming a degenerate triangle (a line segment), not a triangle with zero area in the usual sense.  ·  You can use the triangle law for more than two vectors directly — The triangle law is specifically for two vectors. For three or more, you apply it successively or use the polygon law. $\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}$ requires two applications of the triangle law.  ·  The order of vectors in the triangle matters for the resultant's direction — The triangle law is commutative: $\vec{P}+\vec{Q} = \vec{Q}+\vec{P}$. Swapping the order just reflects the triangle but gives the same resultant vector.
